members.excerpt: The [public, MIT-licensed project](https://github.com/AnthusAI/Decision-Models-Are-Not-Calculators) has the preregistered question, exact replies, checksummed response files, and code that generated the figures.

These are the actual selected choices and returned per-face probabilities, extracted from the [complete response envelopes](https://github.com/AnthusAI/Decision-Models-Are-Not-Calculators/blob/main/results/examples.json):

We repeated both sets once, making **2,880 requests per model**, as [the release manifest confirms](https://github.com/AnthusAI/Decision-Models-Are-Not-Calculators/blob/main/results/release-manifest.json).
The [preregistered matrix](https://github.com/AnthusAI/Decision-Models-Are-Not-Calculators/blob/main/docs/PREREGISTERED.md) puts each face at each list position exactly 120 times per form and pass.
The [released summary](https://github.com/AnthusAI/Decision-Models-Are-Not-Calculators/blob/main/results/summary.json) supplies every count and mean in this table:
*Source: the [complete model-by-model summary](https://github.com/AnthusAI/Decision-Models-Are-Not-Calculators/blob/main/results/summary.json).*
Kev and Laya both falsified the literal “always one” claim in the [complete record](https://github.com/AnthusAI/Decision-Models-Are-Not-Calculators/blob/main/results/summary.json).

Laya strongly favored six, especially with word labels: its mean returned probability for `six` was **91.8%** in the [first word pass](https://github.com/AnthusAI/Decision-Models-Are-Not-Calculators/blob/main/results/summary.json).
That baseline comes from the [stated fair-die setup](https://github.com/AnthusAI/Decision-Models-Are-Not-Calculators/blob/main/docs/PREREGISTERED.md); the models never observed the roll.

In the first digit pass, Kev picked the **first-listed choice in 426 of 720 orders**—59.2%, where a position-neutral pattern across this balanced set would be 16.7%, according to the [position breakdown](https://github.com/AnthusAI/Decision-Models-Are-Not-Calculators/blob/main/results/summary.json).

Jev always picked face one, which occupied each position 120 times, so its selected-position counts were exactly even in the [same recorded breakdown](https://github.com/AnthusAI/Decision-Models-Are-Not-Calculators/blob/main/results/summary.json).

The [build notes](https://github.com/AnthusAI/Decision-Models-Are-Not-Calculators/blob/main/docs/engines.md) and [release manifest](https://github.com/AnthusAI/Decision-Models-Are-Not-Calculators/blob/main/results/release-manifest.json) record the versions.

Jev rounds probabilities to two decimal places; the [measurement note](https://github.com/AnthusAI/Decision-Models-Are-Not-Calculators/blob/main/docs/measurement-notes.md) explains why we preserved those raw values.

Benford's Law concerns leading digits in some observed datasets, as the [earlier examples](/blog/the-dominance-of-ones/) show.
